paper.title: Search for a Dispersion Measure Excess Toward Nearby Galaxy Halos Using Fast Radio Bursts from the Second CHIME/FRB Baseband Catalog
paper.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) probe foreground ionized baryons via their dispersion measures (DM). Using 1748 sub-arcminute-localized sources from the Second CHIME/FRB Baseband Catalog, we conduct a statistical stacking study of the circumgalactic media (CGM) of nearby galaxies by analyzing the DMs of FRBs whose sightlines intersect foreground halos. For galaxy halos within 50 Mpc, we measure a mean DM excess of $119\pm44$ pc~cm$^{-3}$ $(p = 0.0053; \sim 2.6σ)$ within one virial radius. Expanding to 150 Mpc (628 intersections), we find a tentative decline in the mean DM as a function of impact parameter $(p = 0.0046; \sim 2.6σ)$, which is predominantly driven by typical Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies $(10 \leq \log(M_*/M_\odot)\leq 11)$. We use this DM profile to constrain parameters of the CGM electron density distribution, $n_e^\mathrm{CGM}(r) \propto r^{-3β}$, finding an extrapolated central electron density in the range of $(1.7-21.1) \times 10^{-3}\mathrm{\,cm}^{-3}$, with a radial power-law index of $β= 0.68^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$, consistent with constraints from X-ray stacking studies of MW-like galaxies. At very low impact parameters, we detect a significant DM deficit likely due to cross-matching FRBs that originate from galaxies within our galaxy sample. By deriving the DM-galaxy cross-correlation function, we show that this deficit matches theoretical predictions if 20 FRBs originate from galaxies within 150 Mpc, indicating that CHIME/FRB detects a higher fraction of low-$z$ FRBs than previously thought. We forecast that $10^4$ FRBs with similar localization errors will provide a 5-$σ$ detection of the CGM, and that FRBs at intermediate redshifts ($0.4\lesssim z_\mathrm{FRB}\lesssim 0.75$) are ideal for studying intervening CGMs.

paper.title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Black Holes: Non-Gaussianity and Accretion Evade $μ$-Distortion Constraints
paper.abstract: Recent JWST observations of "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) at $z \gtrsim 4$ suggest the existence of early supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses $\gtrsim 10^6\,M_\odot$. Their rapid emergence challenges conventional seeding and growth scenarios based on accretion and mergers of Population III stellar remnants, motivating renewed interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) formed from primordial perturbations. Explaining such massive seeds requires power spectrum enhancements that are constrained by cosmic microwave background (CMB) spectral distortions. In this work we perform the first comprehensive Bayesian exploration of non-Gaussian primordial perturbations capable of producing SMBH seeds while remaining consistent with CMB spectral distortion constraints, and examine the role of accretion history in constraining these models. We perform a suite of Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses of power spectrum enhancements (lognormal and cut-power-law) with varying local non-Gaussianity and accretion histories, satisfying the COBE/FIRAS $μ$-distortion constraint with and without the requirement that the model produces SMBH seeds. We find that both models can seed LRDs and evade $μ$-distortion bounds for $|f_{\rm NL}|= O(1)$ and peak amplitude $A= O(10^{-3})$, when standard Eddington-limited accretion is also incorporated. Interestingly, the results exhibit a preference for both positive and negative values of $f_{\rm NL}$. The preference for negative $f_{\rm NL}$ is strongly dependent on the accretion history, and is removed if the black holes have a small duty cycle, $f_{\rm duty}\lesssim 0.1$. These results demonstrate that the JWST high-$z$ LRD population can be seeded by primordial perturbations while remaining compatible with CMB data, and highlight the importance of next-generation CMB spectral distortion missions to test this hypothesis.

paper.title: The Brown Dwarf Desert is a Mass-Ratio Desert: Astrometric Demographics of 63,254 Stars
paper.abstract: Brown dwarfs are rare as close companions to stars compared to planets and stellar companions, a paucity known as the brown dwarf desert. Whether the desert sits at a fixed companion mass or a fixed companion-to-star mass-ratio $q$ has been difficult to test, because microlensing, radial velocities, and direct imaging have sampled comparatively narrow slices of stellar mass and separation. Here we apply a novel joint-modelling method to Hipparcos and Gaia DR2/DR3 astrometry from 63,254 stars to complete this picture with a sample 1-2 orders of magnitude larger than those of previous wide-orbit demographic studies. For the first time, we present a single survey that measures occurrence rates of both planetary and stellar companions on 3--94 yr orbits ($\sim$2--20\,au) across host masses from M dwarfs to B stars. We find that the desert is a mass-ratio feature: companions are strongly depleted at $q\approx2\%$ independent of stellar mass from M to B stars, and a desert at fixed companion mass is excluded. Furthermore, we find a positive trend in occurrence with metallicity below the mass-ratio desert, but a negative trend above. The desert therefore separates two distinct populations, plausibly two formation channels, that each scale with stellar mass: the lightest stellar-like companions of K stars ($\sim13 \, M_{jup}$) are less massive than the heaviest planet-like companions of B stars ($\sim27, M_{jup}$), which continue well beyond the deuterium-burning limit. Mass-ratio, not mass, is therefore the physically meaningful boundary between planets and their stellar-like counterparts.
